Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The people responsible have faced no consequences
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Body Shame' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile for a civilian-in-war-zone trauma unless there is some indication of bodily violation, injury, or humiliation. The other selected items center on injustice, impunity, hypervigilance, dissociative/fragmented memory, and avoidance, but provide no supporting context for body-focused shame, making this item stand out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The Threat items emphasize pervasive current danger and hypervigilance (scanning exits, needing to stay alert at night), but the formulation specifically has Triggers → Threat inactive. In this profile, Triggers are concrete reminders such as car sounds and related media, yet the Threat items are generalized and not plausibly linked to those triggers; this makes the threat presentation feel disconnected from the trigger pattern.

vignette:
Khun

Khun was forty-two years old in 1982 when he and his wife Srey finally left Cambodia, though the shelling that had fractured his world had come years earlier, in the late 1970s, during the fighting that consumed Phnom Penh. He had been a welder for the municipal water authority then, a steady man with steady hands, and he had stayed through the early fighting because leaving seemed more dangerous than remaining. The day that changed everything, he was walking home from the market when the first volley came—a sound like the sky cracking open, so loud it seemed to originate inside his own chest rather than from outside. He ran. The street fractured into chaos: people screaming, a child's shoe abandoned on the pavement, the smell of smoke and something else, something burnt that he would later understand was flesh. A building two blocks from where he stood collapsed in a cloud of dust. He made it home. His wife, Srey, was there. They locked the door as if locks mattered. That night, the shelling continued intermittently, and Khun sat by the window in the dark, listening to each distant concussion, trying to calculate whether the next one would be closer. He did not sleep. Within days, they fled, eventually reaching a refugee camp in Thailand before making their way to America with papers and almost nothing else.

Now, at seventy-four, Khun lives in a small house on a tree-lined street in a modest neighborhood. He retired five years ago, though he still takes occasional welding jobs for a contractor he has known for decades. He and Srey have been married for fifty-two years, and they have two adult children and grandchildren. For most of the decades since arriving in America, he functioned. He found work as a welder again—his hands remembered what his mind tried to forget—and he built a life that felt, on the surface, stable and whole. But the past did not dissolve; it only went quiet, waiting. In the last year, something has shifted. He cannot quite articulate what, but the world has begun to feel dangerous again in ways that do not quite make sense to him, and he is terrified by what this might mean.

The car sounds are the worst. A loud engine, a backfire, even the percussive rumble of a delivery truck—anything that carries that sudden, explosive quality—and Khun's body responds as though the shelling has resumed. His heart accelerates, his breath becomes shallow and tight, and for several seconds, he cannot seem to draw air into his lungs properly. The sensation terrifies him. He has come to believe that these episodes are warnings, that his body knows something his mind does not, that the world is as dangerous as it was then and he has somehow fooled himself into thinking otherwise. He avoids driving now, and he has begun to avoid the main roads near his house. When Srey needs to go to the grocery store, he waits inside rather than accompany her, claiming fatigue. He no longer sits on the front porch in the evenings as he once did. The open space of the street, the exposure of being visible from the road, fills him with an unnamed dread that he cannot justify but cannot shake. His concentration has become unreliable. He will begin reading the newspaper and find that he has turned three pages without retaining a word. At night, he lies awake beside Srey, his mind alert and scanning, certain that something requires his vigilance. He does not know what. Sleep, when it comes, is shallow and interrupted. He wakes at small sounds—the house settling, a car passing—and it takes him long minutes to remember where he is, who he is, that he is safe.

What troubles him most is the quality of his own memories. He can see fragments—the dust, Srey's face in the doorway, the sound—but they feel discontinuous, as though someone else experienced them and he is simply watching from a distance. The whole thing seems impossible now, too extreme to have actually happened, and yet he carries a certainty that it was his fault somehow, that he made choices that day that brought the danger to his door, that he failed to protect what mattered. No one has ever been held accountable for what occurred. The injustice of that sits in his chest like a stone. When his daughter, Sophea, asked him recently about his reluctance to attend his grandson's school event in the gymnasium, Khun told her he was unwell. He could not explain that the thought of sitting in that large, open room—surrounded by people, with exits he would have to navigate—made him feel trapped in a way that contradicted itself. She did not press him, but he saw the worry in her face. He has said almost nothing to Srey about what he is experiencing. When she asks if something is wrong, he redirects, telling her about the news or asking about her day. The truth feels too large to speak aloud, and he is ashamed of it—this fear that has returned after forty years, this sense that he is not safe even now, even here, even at seventy-four.

Last month, when a documentary about Southeast Asian conflicts came on television, Khun left the room without explanation. Srey found him in the garage an hour later, sitting in the dark. That night, he finally told her that he wanted to speak to someone. He did not know what help might look like, but he could no longer carry this alone. At his age, he had thought he was finished with the war. He is beginning to understand that the war, in some form, has never finished with him.
